\begin{document}

\title{Boundary Veto: Model-Free Post-Processing for Agricultural Field Boundary Delineation}
\author{Aviskar~Giri and Isaac~Corley%
\thanks{The authors are with Taylor Geospatial, St.\ Louis, MO 63108 USA
(e-mail: aviskar.giri@taylorgeospatial.org).}}
\markboth{IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters}%
{Giri and Corley: Boundary Veto for Agricultural Field Boundary Delineation}
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Field boundary networks predict background, field interior, and boundary classes, but those pixels must become polygons to describe individual fields.
On Fields of The World, discarding boundary-class pixels removes thin and small fields, while a watershed, which grows regions from seed points, cuts fields at narrow points without predicted boundaries.
Merging those regions back recovers the accuracy but throws away the correct splits with the wrong ones.
We introduce the \emph{boundary veto}, which keeps every non-background pixel and rejects a proposed split unless boundary probability is at least equal to field probability along most of its line.
The test compares two of the network's own probabilities at one pixel, so the veto needs three constants, no weight changes, and no reference polygons at inference.
Across ten held-out countries, polygon-level panoptic quality (PQ), which combines field detection and shape accuracy, rises by \GainMin{} to \GainMax{} points over the conversion released with Fields of the Planet (FTP), with the same minimum-size step.
The comparison covers two encoders, which extract image features, and two sensors, PlanetScope and Sentinel-2, with improvements in \UpTotal{} of 40 country and model pairs at \OursSlowdown{} the FTP conversion's runtime on the densest patches.
Most of the gain comes from fields under 0.5~ha, the ones a field-class foreground most often loses and the ones smallholder mapping depends on.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
Agricultural field delineation, instance segmentation, watershed transform, post-processing, remote sensing.
\end{IEEEkeywords}

\section{Introduction}
\IEEEPARstart{F}{ield} polygons are the reporting unit for crop area, yield, and management practices, so a field boundary model is only useful once its pixel predictions become one polygon per field.
Public benchmarks now cover this task at 10~m with Sentinel-2~\cite{kerner2024ftw,dandrimont2023ai4boundaries,persello2023ai4smallfarms} and at 3~m with PlanetScope~\cite{corley_ftp}.
Models trained on them predict three classes, background, field interior, and boundary~\cite{waldner2020decode,waldner2020edge,kerner2024ftw,muhawenayo2026prue}, most recently for a global map at 10~m~\cite{ftw_global}.
The FTP conversion~\cite{corley_ftp} uses only field-class pixels as its foreground, the pixels available to form polygons.
Its watershed~\cite{soille2004morphological} starts at peaks in the distance to the nearest predicted boundary pixel~\cite{waldner2020decode,corley_ftp} and uses that distance to divide the foreground.
Before extracting polygons, it merges adjacent regions into connected components, groups of touching pixels.
The global map~\cite{ftw_global} skips the watershed and extracts connected components of the field class directly.

\label{fig:gallery}

Both conversions discard boundary-class pixels, so a narrow field or one with uncertain edges disappears when the boundary class covers it (Fig.~\ref{fig:gallery}).
On PlanetScope with the B3 model, \BaseMiss\% of reference fields have no prediction covering half of their area, and the FTP conversion predicts fewer fields than the reference in all ten countries.
The watershed introduces another error by placing lines at narrow points in the foreground without checking for a predicted boundary.
Its regions score \RawInstPQ{} PQ against \CCPQ{} for connected components of the same foreground.
Merging the regions back recovers that accuracy, but the FTP conversion then loses every correct split as well.

We keep boundary-class pixels so that thin and small fields can form polygons, then use the network's boundary probabilities to decide which watershed lines to keep.
A line's \emph{support} is the fraction of its pixels where boundary probability is at least equal to field probability, and we keep it only when support reaches $\tau$.
Otherwise, we veto the split and merge the two regions.
The split test asks only which of the two classes scores higher at a pixel, so rescaling both probabilities the same way leaves every decision unchanged.
We change no weights and add no training stage, so the boundary veto applies to any three-class field boundary model for tens of milliseconds of extra work per patch.
We keep the released seed-selection depth of $h=2$ and remove the smallest polygons at the end, a minimum-size step any conversion can apply.
All three constants stay the same for every country and sensor.

We evaluate on the ten densely annotated held-out countries of Fields of The World~\cite{kerner2024ftw} with the released EfficientNet~\cite{tan2019efficientnet} U-Nets~\cite{ronneberger2015unet} for PlanetScope~\cite{corley_ftp} and Sentinel-2~\cite{kerner2024ftw}, scored against the reference polygons.
With the same minimum-size step, the boundary veto gains \GainMin{} to \GainMax{} PQ points averaged over countries across two encoders and two sensors, improving \UpTotal{} of the 40 country and model pairs.
Selecting the best watershed depth per country on the test labels recovers less than a third of that gain (Sec.~\ref{sec:results}).

\section{Related Work}
Field delineation from satellite imagery has moved from edge detection and region growing~\cite{wagner2020growing} to fully convolutional networks that predict boundary and interior classes~\cite{persello2019delineation,waldner2020decode,waldner2020edge}.
Benchmark datasets now provide common annotations and evaluation procedures~\cite{kerner2024ftw,dandrimont2023ai4boundaries,persello2023ai4smallfarms,corley_ftp}.
\emph{A Practical Recipe for Field Boundary Segmentation at Scale} (PRUE)~\cite{muhawenayo2026prue} compared encoders, decoders that turn features into pixel predictions, and training recipes on Fields of The World and found that a U-Net with an EfficientNet encoder remains the most accurate choice.
Fields of the Planet~\cite{corley_ftp} reports that these three-class networks outperform the Delineate Anything instance models~\cite{lavreniuk2025delineateanything}, in both their first and second versions, on the same held-out countries.
For buildings, polygon extraction uses frame fields, which encode edge directions, or graph networks, which connect predicted vertices~\cite{girard2021framefield,zorzi2022polyworld,zorzi2020regularization}.
The released field models on these benchmarks still assign pixels to three classes before a watershed or connected components produce polygons, so improving that conversion benefits the current best models without retraining.

Hierarchical merging combines regions in order of border strength until a threshold is reached~\cite{arbelaez2011hierarchical,maninis2018cob}, as Persello et al.~\cite{persello2019delineation} do for field boundaries.
Stochastic watershed estimates boundary probability by repeating the watershed with randomly sampled seeds~\cite{angulo2007stochastic}, while iterative marker depth methods adjust seed selection for each region~\cite{koyuncu2016iterative}.
The methods decide splits from one input map or from seed statistics.
By checking each line against the network's boundary probability, we use evidence absent from the distance map while retaining boundary-class pixels in the foreground.

\section{Method}
\label{sec:method}
To recover fields lost during conversion, we start from the network's class probabilities $p_{\mathrm{bg}}, p_{\mathrm{field}}, p_{\mathrm{bnd}}$ for one image (Fig.~\ref{fig:pipeline}).
The boundary veto uses only the most probable class at each pixel, written $\arg\max p$, and the field and boundary probabilities to produce field polygons.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{rev_method.pdf}
\caption{\textbf{The boundary veto keeps boundary-class pixels and rejects splits without predicted boundaries.}
The pixels the network assigns to the boundary class, orange in (c), are the ones the FTP conversion drops from the foreground and the boundary veto keeps.
A watershed over the distance to the predicted boundary (d) proposes too many splits (e) because it cuts at every narrow point.
Colors show support for each proposed line (f), with blue lines following predicted boundaries and red lines crossing fields.
The veto keeps the blue lines and removes the red ones to produce one polygon per field (g), with the reference outlined in black.
Rows are dense crops, two from PlanetScope and one from Sentinel-2.}
\label{fig:pipeline}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph{Foreground}
We use $F=\{\arg\max p \neq \mathrm{bg}\}$ as the foreground, keeping both field and boundary classes.
Boundary pixels can then connect neighboring fields, so the watershed must separate them before we extract polygons.

\paragraph{Split Proposals}
Let $D$ be the straight-line distance from each pixel to the nearest pixel with $\arg\max p = \mathrm{bnd}$, set to zero outside $F$.
We place seeds at the $h$-maxima of $D$, peaks that stand at least $h=2$ pixels above their surroundings, and run a watershed of $-D$ within $F$~\cite{soille2004morphological}.
Unlike the FTP conversion, we retain the one-pixel lines between regions.
The watershed cuts at every narrow point in the foreground, leaving the veto to reject unnecessary splits.

\paragraph{The Veto}
For each line $\ell$ separating two regions, we compute support as
\begin{equation}
s(\ell)=\frac{1}{|\ell|}\sum_{x\in\ell}\mathbf{1}\left[p_{\mathrm{bnd}}(x)\geq p_{\mathrm{field}}(x)\right],
\label{eq:support}
\end{equation}
where $\mathbf{1}[\cdot]$ equals one when the comparison holds and zero otherwise.
We keep a line with $s(\ell)\geq\tau$ as a one-pixel gap between fields, but remove one with $s(\ell)<\tau$ and merge the two regions.
Regions joined by vetoed lines form groups, and we apply all line decisions together.
A line pixel can be filled only when every region it touches joins the same group and no neighboring line pixel would join a different group.
We use $\tau=0.7$, and values from 0.7 to 0.9 change the result by at most half a point (Sec.~\ref{sec:ablation}).

\paragraph{Polygons}
We trace each field's pixel boundary as a polygon without simplifying it.
The one-pixel gaps keep neighbors distinct when the polygons are converted back to pixels on the same grid.
We then drop fields smaller than 900~m$^2$.
The threshold gives the FTP conversion its highest validation score, while the boundary veto's validation score varies by less than half a point between 450 and 1800~m$^2$ (supplementary material).
We specify the threshold in ground area rather than pixels to give it the same meaning on either sensor.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

\paragraph{Data}
We use the test split of the ten densely annotated held-out countries of Fields of The World~\cite{kerner2024ftw}, named in Fig.~\ref{fig:percountry}, with 2,544 PlanetScope patches at 3~m~\cite{corley_ftp} and 3,034 Sentinel-2 patches.
We exclude Kenya because only some fields are annotated.
PlanetScope covers only the subset with an aligned PlanetScope image, so we compare each sensor against its own baseline.
We score against the released reference polygons clipped to each patch, rather than class labels on a pixel grid.

\paragraph{Models}
We run the EfficientNet-B3 and B7 U-Nets of Fields of the Planet for PlanetScope~\cite{corley_ftp} and of Fields of The World for Sentinel-2~\cite{kerner2024ftw}.
We use the released weights and average predictions over eight flips and rotations, following the released inference settings.
Sentinel-2 images are distributed on a 256$\times$256 grid per patch, so the ground area per pixel varies with latitude.
The vector labels are not confined to the sensor's 10~m pixel grid, and the released model was trained to predict on the same finer grid.
Following the released evaluation, we double the grid resolution and score on that finer grid without changing any weights.

\paragraph{Baselines}
We reproduce the FTP conversion using the field class, watershed depth $h=2$, and connected components of the combined regions.
Our per-country PQ agrees with the reported scores to within $10^{-3}$ for PlanetScope~\cite{corley_ftp} and Sentinel-2~\cite{kerner2024ftw}.
For Sentinel-2, we check that agreement on the 10~m grid used by that paper's evaluation.
To measure what depth tuning can achieve, we also select each country's best depth in $\{0.5,\ldots,64\}$ using its test labels under the same procedure.
Four prior conversions use the same predictions.
We test field and boundary probability thresholds~\cite{waldner2020decode} and hierarchical merging by mean boundary probability along shared borders~\cite{arbelaez2011hierarchical,maninis2018cob,persello2019delineation}, along with stochastic watershed~\cite{angulo2007stochastic} and iterative marker depth~\cite{koyuncu2016iterative}.
For each, we search its parameter grid on PlanetScope B3 and report test results for the setting with the highest country-averaged score on the \emph{validation} split.
We use the same selection rule for the boundary veto and reuse the chosen settings unchanged on Sentinel-2.

\paragraph{Metrics}
We pair predicted and reference polygons one at a time at intersection over union (IoU) 0.5, where IoU is their shared area divided by their combined area.
Every method compared here partitions the foreground, so predictions never overlap and each reference field pairs with at most one of them.
Recognition quality (RQ) measures field detection as the number of matched polygons divided by the average number of predicted and reference polygons.
Segmentation quality (SQ) measures shape accuracy as the mean IoU of matched polygons, and we compute PQ as their product~\cite{kirillov2019panoptic}.
We pool patches within each country, then give all ten countries equal weight in the macro average.
We also report PQ and RQ over the reference parcels under 0.5~ha, the small bin of the FTP evaluation code and the largest of its three bins.
The miss rate is the fraction of reference fields with no prediction covering half of their area, and the merge rate the fraction of predictions covering half of two or more reference fields.
All values are on a 0--100 scale.

\subsection{Results}
\label{sec:results}
The boundary veto raises PQ on all four model and sensor pairs with the same minimum-size step as the FTP conversion (Table~\ref{tab:main}).
Even selecting each country's best watershed depth on its test labels produces a smaller gain (Table~\ref{tab:compare}, $\Delta$tune).
SQ and RQ improve along with small-field PQ, while the miss rate falls on every pair and the merge rate changes by at most 1.5 points in either direction.
The largest improvements occur in the smallest fields (Table~\ref{tab:main}), where smallholder mapping needs them~\cite{persello2023ai4smallfarms}.
On PlanetScope B3, PQ below 0.5~ha rises from 15.7 to 20.5, compared with 52.0 to 53.4 above 2~ha, with the same ordering on all four pairs (supplementary material).
Cambodia has the smallest fields and gains most on average over the four pairs, while Portugal, with two test patches, has the only pair that decreases (Fig.~\ref{fig:percountry}).

\subsection{Comparison with Prior Post-Processing}
\label{sec:compare}
The boundary veto is the only conversion that exceeds the FTP conversion on these predictions (Table~\ref{tab:compare}).
Thresholding the two probability maps gives the highest accuracy and lowest cost among prior conversions, but it leaves neighboring fields merged wherever a predicted boundary has a gap, which is what a watershed can separate.
Hierarchical merging resembles the boundary veto because both score borders by boundary probability, but it uses an absolute threshold while we compare probabilities at the same pixel.
Selecting each country's best setting using its own test labels instead of the shared setting adds \OursTune{} points to the boundary veto and at most \PriorTuneMax{} to any prior method.
We measure runtime on one core, grouping PlanetScope patches by the number of reference fields they contain.
On Sentinel-2, every method takes longer on the larger grid, and the ordering on dense patches is unchanged (supplementary material).
The boundary veto takes \OursSlowdown{} the FTP conversion's time on dense patches, while stochastic watershed is \SwstSlowdown{} slower still because it repeats the watershed for each set of seeds.
Every method uses less than \PeakMB{}~MB of additional memory per patch on either sensor, so runtime determines the choice.

\subsection{Ablation}
\label{sec:ablation}
Keeping boundary-class pixels without splitting merges neighboring fields and lowers PQ to \NbgNonePQ{} (Table~\ref{tab:ablation}).
Conversely, the split rule adds nothing to the field-class foreground because gaps left by the boundary class already separate most fields.
The supplementary sweeps show at most half a point of variation for $\tau$ between 0.7 and 0.9.
With $h=1$, PQ falls by about one point, with $h=4$ by one to two, and with $h=8$ it falls because small fields lose their seeds.
Three alternatives to the most probable class also failed: Otsu thresholding, which separates low from high field probabilities automatically, morphological closing, which fills gaps in the boundary class, and a watershed driven by boundary probability in place of distance.
All three score below the FTP conversion on both splits (supplementary material).
Requiring longer kept lines, testing support over a band around each line, or merging thin regions into a neighbor each lowered validation accuracy.
Filling holes inside a field changed the validation score by less than a tenth of a point.
Only the minimum-size step helps among the additions, improving the FTP conversion by \BaseAreaGain{} points against \OursAreaGain{} for the boundary veto on PlanetScope B3.
The released polygon extraction tool~\cite{kerner2024ftw} includes this threshold, although the published evaluation does not apply one.

\section{Conclusion}
The boundary veto uses boundary-class pixels to recover discarded fields and boundary probabilities to decide which watershed splits to keep.
Together, those changes improve polygon accuracy over the FTP conversion on two encoders and two sensors without per-region tuning, with the largest gain in the small fields needed for smallholder mapping.
The rule needs a predicted boundary class, so it does not apply to instance segmentation models that return only masks and scores, and we score Sentinel-2 on the finer grid the model and the vector labels resolve rather than on native 10~m pixels.
Fields the network misses entirely cannot be recovered by reorganizing its predicted pixels.
